To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(i) the absorption coefficient of whole blood in visible to NIR wavelength range is dominated by hemoglobin, and (ii) the scattering coefficient of whole blood is dominated by red blood cells.

the absorption coefficient of platelets is negligible, the absorption coefficient of red blood cells is 1.6 times larger than that of saline solution, and the effective scattering of red blood cells in saline solution and plasma are the same.

the scattering coefficient and anistropy factor of PLTs increase linearly with the concentration and the scattering coefficient of cell-free plasma is higher than expected for Rayligh scattering by proteins.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the optical behavior of blood and its components.
the optical properties of PLTs suspended in plasma and blood and their influence on whole blood in the spectral range from 450 to 1100 nm.
the optical properties of platelets, blood plasma, and red blood cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the optical properties of PLTs suspended in plasma and blood are not significantly influenced by their environment.

the optical properties of whole blood can be determined accurately by the optical properties of its components, i.e. the optical properties of blood are additive and can be calculated by the optical properties and volume fractions of the single blood components.

red blood cells are the dominant scattering and absorbing component of whole blood in a wide range of wavelengths and that the scattering behavior of PLTs can be described by a linear dependence on the PLT concentration.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the optical properties of PLTs are of minor importance in the visible to NIR range.
PLTs have to be considered as a blood constituent for the determination of optical parameters of whole blood.
PLTs are the most important scattering component in whole blood in the wavelength range from 600 nm to 900 nm, whereas in the visible wavelength range, the scattering by red blood cells dominates.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the scattering properties of PLTs have to be taken into account when modeling the optical properties of blood.
the scattering coefficient of PLT suspensions is significantly higher than expected from Rayleigh scattering.
in order to accurately model the optical properties of whole blood, the scattering behavior of PLTs needs to be included in addition to the absorption and scattering by red blood cells.
